_comment: The five acts of the ANE Atlas. years are BCE (1200 = older, 539 = newer). focus is a [[swLat, swLng], [neLat, neLng]] Leaflet bounds box. Narrative quotes are drawn from the study library; see 07-study-library for sourcing.

acts.title: Collapse & Emergence
acts.subtitle: The Bronze Age collapse empties the coasts. The highlands fill with farmers.
acts.narrative: The great empires of the Late Bronze Age — Hittite, Mycenaean, Egyptian — shatter between 1200 and 1150 BCE. In the wreckage, Canaan's coastal cities empty out. The highlands of the interior see a population boom: indigenous farmers abandoning the crumbling city-states for the safety of the hills. These highland villagers are the people the Bible calls Israel. In the deep south, Egyptian texts already know a people called the Shasu of Yhw — semi-nomadic herders who carry the name of a god named Yahweh.

acts.title: The United Monarchy
acts.subtitle: One kingdom — or two very different stories about a small highland town.
acts.narrative: The Bible tells of a golden empire: David ruling from Dan to Beersheba, Solomon's temple, 700 wives, tribute from every direction. Archaeology tells a smaller story: a highland town of a few thousand people at Jerusalem, a modest chiefdom, and Canaanite city-states like Megiddo and Gezer still independent and still rich. The toggle is the whole point of this act — the same ground, two very different kingdoms.

acts.title: The Rival Kingdoms
acts.subtitle: A rich north, a scrappy south, and scribes who hated the north.
acts.narrative: After Solomon the kingdom splits. Israel in the north is larger, richer, sits on the Via Maris trade route, and builds real cities — Samaria, the work of the Omride dynasty. Assyrian records call it the House of Omri. Judah in the south is a poor hill-country backwater, saved by one asset: the House of David, which will rule for 400 years. The Bible — written and edited by Judahite scribes — condemns every northern king as evil. The crime: rival shrines at Dan and Bethel, where golden calves stood under Yahweh, not in place of him.

acts.title: The Assyrian Shadow
acts.subtitle: The empire that erased Israel — and the vassal that survived by paying.
acts.narrative: Assyria — ruthless, bureaucratic, utterly dominant — destroys the northern kingdom in 722 BCE and deports its elite, creating the legend of the Ten Lost Tribes. Judah survives only as a vassal. Hezekiah rebels and nearly dies for it: Sennacherib's prism records how he shut up Hezekiah 'like a bird in a cage.' Then Assyria itself collapses — civil war, drought, and a Babylonian-Median coalition that sacks Nineveh in 612. A power vacuum opens, and King Josiah of Judah runs into it.

acts.title: Babylonian Fall & Exile
acts.subtitle: The temple burns, the elite are carried off — and the pen wins the war.
acts.narrative: Babylon defeats Egypt at Carchemish and becomes the new superpower. When Judah rebels, Nebuchadnezzar smashes Jerusalem in 586 BCE and deports the elite in three waves. The exiles were not all Yahwists — they were the wealthy, including syncretists and polytheists. Only the strict Yahwist faction survived culturally, and they used the trauma to reinterpret everything: we were punished because we worshipped other gods. They lost the war, lost the land, lost the temple — and won the pen. When Cyrus of Persia conquers Babylon in 539 and lets the exiles return, they come back carrying the scrolls that become Judaism.
